body:
Why Jainism and Buddhism are compared

Jainism and Buddhism developed in the same broad historical environment and addressed related questions about suffering, rebirth, karma, moral responsibility and liberation. Both questioned the religious authority of the Vedas and taught that an individual's conduct matters.

These similarities are substantial, but they do not make the 2 traditions doctrinally identical. Their most important differences concern the existence of the soul, the nature of karma and the appropriate path to liberation.

Point-by-point doctrinal comparison

AspectJainismBuddhism
Important teacherMahavira, the 24th TirthankaraGautama Buddha
Earlier traditionRecognises 23 Tirthankaras before MahaviraGautama Buddha is the central teacher of the historical Buddhist tradition
Vedic authorityDoes not accept the Vedas as supreme religious authorityDoes not accept the Vedas as supreme religious authority
Individual soulAccepts an enduring individual JivaTeaches Anatta, the absence of an eternal individual self
Nature of realityRecognises enduring substances with changing modes and many-sided descriptionsEmphasises impermanence and conditioned existence
KarmaSubtle karmic matter binds the soulIntentional actions have consequences without an eternal soul
RebirthAccepts rebirth under karmic bondageAccepts rebirth through conditioned continuity
Principal Jain or Buddhist frameworkTriratna and the 5 vowsFour Noble Truths and Noble Eightfold Path
Path of disciplineStrong emphasis on renunciation and severe ascetic restraintMiddle Way between self-indulgence and severe self-mortification
Non-violenceExceptionally strict Ahimsa towards living beingsNon-harming, compassion and ethical conduct
LiberationMoksha: freedom of the enduring soul from karma and rebirthNirvana: cessation of craving and the conditions sustaining suffering and rebirth
Monastic organisationJain monks and nuns; lay supportersBuddhist Sangha of monks and nuns; lay supporters
Distinctive doctrinesAnekantavada and SyadvadaFour Noble Truths, Middle Way, Anicca and Anatta

The central difference: Jiva and Anatta

Jainism teaches that every living being possesses an enduring individual soul. Karmic bondage prevents the soul from realising its pure nature. Through right understanding and disciplined conduct, the soul can become free from karma.

Buddhism rejects an unchanging individual self. It regards bodily and mental experiences as conditioned and impermanent. Karma and rebirth still operate, but Buddhism does not explain them by assuming that a permanent soul moves unchanged between bodies.

Jainism accepts an enduring Jiva. Buddhism teaches Anatta, or non-self. Both accept karma and rebirth, but their explanations of personal continuity differ.

The difference between the 2 sets of 3 jewels

The expression Triratna means 3 jewels and appears in discussions of both religions. Its contents must be identified from the religious context.

Jain Triratna

  • Right Faith or Samyak Darshana.
  • Right Knowledge or Samyak Jnana.
  • Right Conduct or Samyak Charitra.

Buddhist 3 jewels

  • Buddha, the enlightened teacher.
  • Dhamma or Dharma, the teaching.
  • Sangha, the community.

The Jain 3 jewels describe essential elements of the path to liberation. The Buddhist 3 jewels identify the objects of refuge. They should not be substituted for one another.

The difference in ascetic practice

Jainism treats rigorous self-control and asceticism as central means of overcoming karmic bondage. The ideal ascetic practises very strict non-violence, renunciation and restraint.

The Buddha also taught discipline, but rejected severe self-mortification as an effective path to enlightenment. His Middle Way combines ethical conduct, wisdom and mental development through the Noble Eightfold Path.

This is a difference in religious discipline, not a contrast between a disciplined religion and an undisciplined one.

The difference between Jain and Buddhist liberation

Both traditions seek freedom from the cycle of rebirth. However, they explain the final state through different doctrines.

In Jainism, the individual soul is liberated when its karmic bondage has been completely removed. The soul remains an enduring liberated reality.

In Buddhism, Nirvana signifies the ending of craving, ignorance and the conditions that perpetuate suffering and rebirth. It is not described as the liberation of an eternal individual soul, because the doctrine of Anatta rejects that premise.

Distinguishing closely related terms

TermCorrect association
AnekantavadaJain doctrine of many-sided reality
SyadvadaJain doctrine of conditional predication
JivaEnduring individual soul accepted in Jainism
AnattaBuddhist doctrine of non-self
AniccaBuddhist doctrine of impermanence
MahavrataGreat vow observed by Jain ascetics
Middle WayBuddhist rejection of self-indulgence and extreme self-mortification
TanhaCraving associated with the origin of suffering in Buddhism
Kevala JnanaPerfect knowledge in Jainism

Understanding statements that contain common misconceptions

Both religions reject the Vedas as supreme authority

This is a genuine similarity. Both Jainism and Buddhism developed religious teachings that did not depend on accepting Vedic sacrifices or the Vedas as the final authority.

Only Jainism accepts karma

This is incorrect. Both religions accept karma and rebirth. What differs is the philosophical explanation of how karma operates.

Buddhism rejects the soul, so it also rejects rebirth

This is incorrect. The Buddhist doctrine of non-self rejects a permanent individual soul, not the causal continuity associated with karma and rebirth.

Both religions teach strict asceticism in exactly the same way

This is incorrect. Jainism is particularly associated with rigorous ascetic practice, whereas the Buddha taught a Middle Way rejecting extreme bodily mortification.

Both religions have the same Triratna

This is incorrect. Jain Triratna consists of Right Faith, Right Knowledge and Right Conduct. The Buddhist 3 jewels are Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha.

Final synthesis

Jainism and Buddhism share a concern with moral conduct, the consequences of action, freedom from rebirth and the possibility of individual spiritual progress. Both emerged from the religious discussions of early historic India and developed monastic and lay communities.

However, Jainism explains liberation through the purification of an enduring soul and emphasises strict ascetic restraint. Buddhism explains liberation without an eternal self and teaches the Noble Eightfold Path as the Middle Way.

The distinction between Jain Anekantavada and Syadvada, the distinction between the 2 sets of 3 jewels, and the distinction between Jain Jiva and Buddhist Anatta are especially useful for correctly interpreting short factual and statement-based prelims questions.

Prelims focus

  • Jainism and Buddhism both accept karma, rebirth and liberation.
  • Both reject the Vedas as supreme religious authority.
  • Jainism accepts an enduring individual soul; Buddhism teaches Anatta.
  • Jainism emphasises rigorous ascetic restraint; Buddhism teaches the Middle Way.
  • Jain Triratna consists of Right Faith, Right Knowledge and Right Conduct.
  • Buddhist 3 jewels are Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha.
  • Trap: Similar religious terms do not always carry identical meanings in Jainism and Buddhism.

[References: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6 History, Chapter 7, New Questions and Ideas, printed pp. 65–72; NCERT, Themes in Indian History Part I, Class 12 History, Theme 4, Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings, sections 2–6, printed pp. 84–94; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Jaina Philosophy, sections 1–3, and The Literal-Nonliteral Distinction in Classical Indian Philosophy, section 4.2, consulted 18 November 2026; Harvard University Pluralism Project, The Dharma: The Teachings of the Buddha, consulted 18 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Both traditions seek liberation, but they differ in their explanation of the self and the path.

title: Jainism and Buddhism Compared: Shared Foundations and Decisive Differences
